t: Random Flip Matrix — Fisher-Yates on a Virtual Grid
o: We must repeatedly return a uniformly random cell that is still 0, flip it to 1, and support a full reset. The naive idea — keep the matrix in memory, pick random cells until we hit a 0 — degrades badly as zeros become scarce (rejection sampling can take many tries). The constraints (m, n up to 10^4 but only 1000 calls) tell us we cannot allocate an m×n array (up to 10^8 cells), so we need an approach whose memory depends only on the number of flips performed. In the example with a 3×1 grid, each flip returns one of the remaining zero cells with equal probability, and reset restores everything.
k: Flattening the m×n grid to indices [0, m*n) lets us treat it as a 1-D sampling problem.
Fisher–Yates-style swapping: pick a random index in [0, total_remaining), swap it with the last remaining index, then shrink the range — every remaining index stays equally likely.
A hash map of 'virtual swaps' gives O(1) memory per flip instead of storing the whole grid.

a.n: Approach 1: Rejection Sampling on a Set of Used Cells
a.i: Keep a set of already-flipped flattened indices. Each flip draws a uniform random integer in [0, m*n); if it was used before, redraw. This is simple and correct since each draw is uniform over all cells, but when few zeros remain the expected number of redraws grows like (m*n)/zeros, which can be huge even though the problem guarantees at most 1000 calls.
s: Flatten cells: index = i * n + j.
Maintain a hash set of used indices.
On flip, repeatedly generate rand() % (m*n) until an unused index appears; add it to the set and decode to [index / n, index % n].
a.t: O(1) expected per flip early on, but O(m*n/zeros) expected per flip near the end — worst case unbounded retries.
a.sp: O(k) where k is the number of flips done since the last reset.

a.n: Approach 2: Fisher–Yates Swap with Hash Map (Optimal)
a.i: Imagine the flattened array [0, m*n). Maintain a shrinking boundary `total` starting at m*n. Pick a uniform random index r in [0, total); the value at position r should be swapped with the value at position total-1, then decrement total. Since we never materialize the array, store only the deviations from identity in a hash map: map[x] holds the value currently at virtual position x (defaulting to x itself). Each remaining index is equally likely because this is exactly one step of Fisher–Yates.
s: Set total = m*n and create an empty map.
flip(): pick r = rand(total); let val = map.getOrDefault(r, r).
Swap: set map[r] = map.getOrDefault(total-1, total-1), decrement total.
reset(): clear the map and restore total = m*n.
a.t: O(1) time per flip and reset — a single random draw plus constant-time hash operations.
a.sp: O(min(1000, m*n)) for the hash map — proportional to the number of flips actually made, never to the grid size.

w: In an interview, mention rejection sampling briefly to show intuition, then present the Fisher–Yates-with-hash-map solution as the answer — it uses exactly one random call per flip and O(#flips) memory, which matches the problem's optimization hints. Pitfalls: forgetting that m*n can exceed 32-bit-safe intermediate values in some languages (use long/Number carefully — here 10^8 fits in int), off-by-one errors when decrementing total before or after reading the swap target (decrement first, then read position total), and decoding back to 2-D coordinates correctly. Edge cases: a 1×1 grid, resetting between flips, and more flips than distinct rows. Follow-ups: how would you handle streaming/reset-heavy workloads (same approach works), or sampling without replacement from a huge unknown universe (reservoir sampling connection).
